title: Antipatterns & Code Review
objective: After this lesson you will be able to spot the nine classic SQL antipatterns in review (SELECT *, blind OFFSET, leading wildcards, OR chains, N+1, implicit conversions, functions on keys, fat joins, magic numbers), explain each one's cost, and prescribe the idiomatic fix.
why: Optimization (Ch.8) fixes slow queries; review prevents them. Seniors spend more time reading SQL than writing it — PRs, ORM output, legacy reports — and the reviewer's value is pattern recognition at speed. This lesson is the checklist that turns 'looks fine' into nine specific, defensible comments.

blocks.text: The review lens: cost, correctness, clarity

Every review comment should name one of three harms. **Cost**: shape/scans the data can't afford (SELECT *, deep OFFSET). **Correctness**: shapes that lie (fanout totals, NULL ambushes, nondeterministic ROW_NUMBER ties). **Clarity**: shapes the next reader will misread (SELECT-list subqueries three deep, magic thresholds). If a comment names none of the three, it's taste — say so or skip it.

rows: Cost + fragility: ships bytes, breaks on schema change
Cost linear in page number + drift
Cost + correctness: index blindness, wrong matches
Match types; CAST the value, never the column
Named CTE/bands table + comment (Ch.2, Ch.5 bands)

blocks.text: Application loops that query per row (`for course: fetch enrollments`) turn one JOIN into N+1 round trips — invisible in development (tiny N), catastrophic in production. In review, any query inside a loop is guilty until proven batched: eager-load with JOINs, `WHERE id IN (…)` batches, or dataloader patterns. The SQL is fine; the call pattern is the bug.

blocks.code:
-- N+1 shape (application pseudocode — the bug lives outside SQL)
-- for c in courses:                      # 1 query
--   n = query("SELECT COUNT(*) … WHERE course_id = ?", c.id)  # +N queries

-- Batched: one grouped query for all courses (real SQLite/PostgreSQL)
-- SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM enrollments
-- WHERE course_id IN (SELECT id FROM courses WHERE published = 1)
-- GROUP BY course_id;
blocks.caption: N+1 dies in batching: IN-list or JOIN replaces the loop

blocks.text: Comparing mismatched types (`WHERE text_id = 5`, dates vs strings) forces conversions that blind indexes *and* change semantics (SQLite's flexible typing is lenient until it isn't; PostgreSQL errors loudly — prefer loud). Rules: schema types correct at DDL time (Chapter 7 of Intermediate), bind parameters with matching types, CAST the literal/value side, never the column side.

blocks.title: The review comment template
blocks.text: File review comments as harm + fix + proof: 'N+1 here (cost: 300 round trips on this page) — batch with WHERE id IN (…) (Ch.3 shapes); verify with the query log count before/after.' Specific, teachable, verifiable — the opposite of 'slow, fix it.'

blocks.query: SELECT id, title, topic FROM courses WHERE published = 1 ORDER BY title LIMIT 5;
blocks.note: Run this clean query in the sandbox — named columns, sargable filter, small LIMIT, meaningful ORDER BY. It is the 'approved' shape: hold every future query against it and name the first deviation.

items: Review through cost/correctness/clarity — comments naming none are taste
N+1 is a call-pattern bug: batch with IN/JOIN, prove with query-log counts
Conversions corrupt silently: correct types at DDL, CAST values never columns
File comments as harm + fix + proof — teachable and verifiable

exercise.prompt: Review this report query and file exactly five comments (harm + fix each): SELECT * FROM courses c, enrollments e WHERE UPPER(c.topic) = 'BACKEND' OR e.progress > 90 ORDER BY e.progress LIMIT 10 OFFSET 500. (a) In the sandbox, run the flat pieces (topic filter, progress filter) and record counts. (b) Write the rescued query for real SQLite/PostgreSQL.
hints: Five findings: comma join (cross-join risk — explicit JOIN … ON), UPPER() on indexed column (sargability — normalize constant), OR across tables (split UNION ALL), OFFSET 500 (keyset), SELECT * (name columns).
Sandbox probes: SELECT title FROM courses WHERE topic = 'backend'; and SELECT COUNT(*) FROM enrollments WHERE progress > 90; — preservation targets for the rewrite.
Rescued shape: explicit JOINs, bare columns, UNION ALL branches with guards, named columns, keyset bookmark, small LIMIT.
exercise.solution:
-- (b) rescued (real SQLite / PostgreSQL)
-- SELECT c.id, c.title, e.progress
-- FROM courses c JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id
-- WHERE c.topic = 'backend' AND e.progress > 90
--   AND (e.progress, e.id) < (?, ?)
-- ORDER BY e.progress DESC, e.id DESC LIMIT 10;
-- (OR-split only if branches need separate indexes; here one sargable AND suffices.)
exercise.why: The exercise compresses the whole gallery into one query: five distinct harms, five fixes, one rescued shape. Real reviews look exactly like this — stacked pathologies in inherited SQL, untangled one harm at a time.

quiz.q: A review comment says only 'this is slow, fix it'. What's wrong with the comment?
options: It names no harm, no fix, no proof — unactionable; good comments state cost/correctness/clarity + remedy + verification
quiz.explain: Review is teaching plus verification. Harm + fix + proof (plan counts, timings, row preservation) makes the comment mergeable wisdom instead of drive-by taste.

quiz.q: Loop of 300 per-row COUNT queries on a page. Diagnosis and fix?
options: N+1: replace with one batched GROUP BY (IN-list or JOIN); prove with query-log counts before/after
quiz.explain: Round trips dominate: 300 queries means 300 network+parse+plan cycles regardless of each query's speed. Batching collapses them to one — the call pattern, not the SQL, was the bug.

quiz.q: WHERE text_id = 5 on a TEXT column is slow and occasionally mismatches. Why?
options: Implicit conversion: per-row casts blind indexes and alter comparison semantics — fix types at DDL, CAST values never columns
quiz.explain: Type mismatches force runtime conversion: index blindness (cost) plus surprising equality rules (correctness). Correctness at DDL time beats cleverness at query time.

options: Ad-hoc exploration in a console/sandbox — then name columns for anything persisted
quiz.explain: SELECT * is an exploration tool: surveying unfamiliar tables interactively. Persisted code (apps, reports, views) names columns — shipping bytes and schema-fragility otherwise.

summary: Review with the gallery memorized: cost (scans, N+1, OFFSET), correctness (conversions, fanout, ties), clarity (magic, nesting). Comment harm + fix + proof, and hold every query against the clean shape.
next: Gallery memorized — now perform the whole craft on one stage. Next and last: the performance-audit capstone walkthrough, then your final assessment.
